A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same task-representation-shift research. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, proofs, figures and tables, support reliable comparison despite substantial revision and reformatting.

before.justification: v2 reports original reinforcement-learning experiments, including update-schedule comparisons, data-quality tests, pretraining comparisons and task-representation visualizations in Figures 2–5.

after.justification: v4 retains original experimental results and adds benchmark evaluations, numerical assumption checks, performance-guided training and CSRO experiments, including Appendix Figures 6–9.

M1.justification: Appendix 8.5.1 adds Performance Control, which uses online evaluations with a pretrained representation to accumulate estimated policy improvements and adapt encoder-update timing. This is a concrete extension of the update gate; the encoder objectives, BRAC policy learning and original fixed schedules remain. Renaming the schedule parameters to Nk and Nacc is otherwise clarification.

E1.justification: Figure 2 and Table 2 add Walker-Param and Push to Ant-Dir, Reach, Dial-Turn and Button-Press, substantially broadening the evaluated locomotion and manipulation tasks. The original environments and Ant-Dir random, medium and expert data conditions are retained.

E2.justification: CSRO moves from cited and theoretically discussed prior work in v2 to an evaluated comparator in v4: Figures 8–9 compare original CSRO with controlled update schedules. The existing contrastive, reconstruction, cross-entropy and pretraining comparisons remain.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce materially different protocols: Appendix 8.3 varies sample size and measures representation discrepancy using MSE, while Appendix 8.5.1 uses online evaluations on three sampled training tasks to guide updates and retains evaluation on twenty test tasks. The original common settings in Table 1 remain unchanged; these additions do not establish reruns or protocol changes for the retained experiments.

E4.justification: v4 adds numerical tests of the sample-size dependence underlying Assumption 4.9 and an experiment testing whether performance feedback can guide encoder updates. Figure 5 also replaces the earlier visualization case study with a different pair of representations evaluated at 300K steps. The existing data-quality and pretraining analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v4 adds paired t-tests and reported p-values against each comparison's worst setting in Table 3, introducing statistical inference across the central results. Eight-seed means and standard-deviation bands already appeared in v2 and remain. The new Performance Control experiment separately reports six seeds; this is not an increase in the original experiments' run count.

E6.justification: v4 adds numerical summaries in Table 3, results for the added environments, assumption-check outcomes, Performance Control results and CSRO curves. For example, its new Walker-Param contrastive comparison reports 299.00 ± 35.42 for the original schedule and 450.47 ± 19.71 for Nk=2, Nacc=1. Figure 5 also replaces the illustrated models and returns; these are different cases, not same-setting performance changes.

T1.justification: Theorems 4.6 and 4.10 and Corollary 6.1 replace the mutual-information-optimal reference with the return-optimal representation. v4 removes the former support-coverage assumption, strengthens Assumption 4.7 to ensure a positive improvement margin, and replaces simplex volume with representation-space cardinality. It also adds Corollary 4.4 with its proof and Appendix 8.3 derivations for alternative approximation-error bounds.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion refine the central problem from performance-improvement collapse toward the insufficiency of a monotonicity condition that ignores representation changes. The principal contributions—identifying task representation shift, deriving conditional guarantees and demonstrating benefits from controlling updates—remain.

C2.justification: v4 adds substantive guidance favoring less frequent encoder updates, expands the pretraining explanation to distinguish approximation error from the gap between mutual-information and return optima, and explicitly acknowledges that policy-learning improvements remain untreated. It also identifies the online Performance Control variant as impractical because of its evaluation cost, materially clarifying applicability limits.

D1.justification: v4 adds a project-code link and a public UNICORN-code link, replacing v2's statement that UNICORN code was obtained from its authors. It clarifies update-frequency semantics and documents new dataset sizes, the controller parameter, NVIDIA 3090 hardware and approximately 3–6-day runtime. Most original architecture, learning-rate and batch-size information is retained.

R1.justification: v4 removes the broad Offline RL and Meta RL related-work paragraphs and their associated citations, while adding works by Li et al. (2021) and Zhang et al. (2024). It also revises the ContrBAR comparison from an OMRL framework-specific guarantee to an online, approximation-specific result contrasted with this paper's broader offline formulation.

P1.justification: Sections 4.2, 4.3 and 6.1 undergo substantial explanatory rewrites. v4 consolidates related work, moves objective descriptions into Appendix 8.4, makes encoder parameterization and schedule terminology more explicit, and reorganizes the appendix around proofs, assumption justification, implementation and additional results. These changes substantially reshape the exposition.

P2.justification: v4 redraws Figure 1, expands Figure 2 from twelve to eighteen panels, replaces Figure 5, and adds Figures 6–9 and the numerical results Table 3. It also expands Table 2, changes legends and captions, relocates existing displays and adopts the ICLR page layout. The visual revision extends well beyond numerical updates or renumbering.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially improves scrutiny of the central guarantee through revised assumptions, an explicit comparison condition, additional derivations and numerical checks of an assumption only briefly justified in v2. Added task and CSRO evaluations, exact result summaries and significance tests strengthen the empirical support, while clearer implementation information and limitations improve assessability. The gains remain qualified: the tests compare against worst settings, and the adaptive controller requires expensive online evaluations rather than providing a practical fully offline solution.
